raw_text:
Below is a single, coach‑friendly 12‑week program you can give your 27‑year‑old beginner client training in a small flat with only a yoga mat and a doorway pull‑up bar. It integrates the strength plan (progressive bodyweight + backpack loading), nutrition guidance, at‑home cardio, push intensity in Phase 2, Saturday finisher, equipment buying path, and daily mobility. I present a week‑by‑week summary with session breakdowns, progression rules, and practical coaching notes so you can deliver it remotely.

Quick overview
- Frequency: 4 strength sessions/week + Saturday finisher. Optional cardio on Wed and/or Sun depending on goals.
- Split: Upper A (Mon), Lower A (Tue), Upper B (Thu), Lower B (Sat morning) + Saturday finisher (later) OR Lower B + finisher same day (shorter). Mobility daily (short) + longer 1–2× week.
- Phases:
  - Phase 1 Foundation: Weeks 1–4 — build movement patterns, volume, technique.
  - Phase 2 Build: Weeks 5–8 — increase push intensity, harder variations, more mechanical tension.
  - Phase 3 Intensify/Peak: Weeks 9–12 — lower‑rep strength emphasis, backpack loading, deload/test Week 12.
- Equipment: mat + pull‑up bar. Recommended purchases across program: backpack, resistance bands, adjustable dumbbells/kettlebells later (see Equipment section).
- Nutrition: three options (surplus for strength, maintenance, deficit). Protein 1.6–2.2 g/kg, creatine 3–5 g/day optional. If you provide his bodyweight I will customise exact kcal/macros.

Progression rules (use weekly)
- Progress when client completes upper target reps/sets with good form for 2 consecutive sessions.
- If stuck, increase volume (more sets), extend eccentric tempo, or add backpack/band assistance/resistance.
- Monitor RPE and recovery; back off volume if performance drops or sleep/energy suffers.

How to read daily session entries
- Warm‑up: 5–8 min dynamic warm‑up each session.
- Main: core strength movements with sets × reps and tempo or cues.
- Accessory: supporting movements for balance/hypertrophy.
- Finish/mobility: short mobility or conditioning as written.
- Rest guidelines: heavy sets 90–180 s; accessory 45–90 s.

Phase 1 — Foundation (Weeks 1–4)
Goal: teach/brake down movement patterns, increase base strength and work capacity.

Weekly layout (Mon/Tue/Thu/Sat + Sat finisher)
- Mon — Upper A (vertical pull + horizontal push focus)
- Tue — Lower A (squat + hinge)
- Wed — Cardio LISS 20–30 min (optional)
- Thu — Upper B (vertical pull + horizontal push variant + horizontal pull)
- Fri — Rest / mobility
- Sat — Lower B (single‑leg focus + core) + Saturday finisher (fun 12–16 min)
- Sun — Rest or light walk & mobility

Week 1 (template for Weeks 1–2; Week 3–4 progression notes after)
Mon — Upper A
- Warm‑up: 5–8 min (arm circles, scapular pull‑ups 2×8, bandless pull‑aparts with towel)
- Main:
  1) Assisted negatives pull‑ups: 4×3–6 (3–5s eccentric). If full pull‑ups possible: 4×3–5.
  2) Incline push‑ups (hands elevated): 4×8–12.
  3) Doorway/inverted row: 3×8–12.
- Accessory:
  4) Pike push‑up progressions: 3×6–8.
  5) Plank: 3×30–45s.
- Finish: pec doorway stretch 2×30s each.

Tue — Lower A
- Warm‑up: leg swings, glute bridges
- Main:
  1) Bulgarian split squat (rear foot elevated): 4×6–10 per leg.
  2) Glute bridge (double or single leg regressions): 4×8–12.
  3) Hip hinge patterning (backpack suitcase deadlift or slow bodyweight hinge): 3×8–12 (3s eccentric).
- Accessory:
  4) Calf raises 3×12–20.
  5) Side plank 3×20–30s per side.
- Finish: hamstring mobility.

Thu — Upper B
- Warm‑up: as Mon
- Main:
  1) Assisted pull‑ups/negatives: 4×4–7.
  2) Push‑ups (standard or knees): 4×8–15 (use 3s eccentric if easy).
  3) Inverted rows: 3×10–12.
- Accessory:
  4) Diamond/close push‑ups: 3×8–12.
  5) Hollow holds/dead bugs: 3×20–30s.
- Finish: scapular pull‑ups 2×8.

Sat — Lower B + core + Finisher
- Warm‑up
- Main:
  1) Bodyweight squats or backpack goblet substitute: 4×12–20.
  2) Reverse or stationary lunges: 3×8–12 per leg.
  3) Hip thrust / single‑leg glute bridge: 4×8–12.
- Accessory:
  4) Nordic progression or 45° back extension substitute: 3×5–8.
  5) Farmer carry with backpack: 2×60s.
- Finish: Saturday finisher (see Saturday finisher section below). Cool down mobility.

Weeks 3–4 progression (Phase 1)
- Increase reps/sets slightly and aim for improving technique. Start moving assisted pull‑up -> banded or partial concentric + eccentric. Add one extra set to main lifts on Week 4 if recovery permits.

Phase 2 — Build (Weeks 5–8)
Goal: increase intensity, especially push work (set/rep reductions, harder variations, pauses/slow eccentrics), increase single‑leg and pulling intensity.

Key changes from Phase 1
- Push intensity: two push sessions/week with 4–6 sets of 4–6 reps on hardest variation; slow eccentrics, 1–3s pauses, rest 90–150 s (detailed push progressions implemented).
- Pulls: progress to more full pull‑ups, banded or unassisted, increase sets.
- Lower: progress toward single‑leg pistols, heavier single‑leg RDLs with backpack.
- Cardio: increase to 2 sessions/week (one LISS + one short HIIT) if conditioning/fat loss is goal; otherwise keep 1 LISS.

Weeks 5–8 weekly template (Mon/Tue/Thu/Sat + Sat finisher)
- Mon — Upper A (horizontal heavy)
- Tue — Lower A (single‑leg + hinge load)
- Wed — Cardio (LISS/MISS) + mobility
- Thu — Upper B (vertical heavy + pull)
- Fri — Rest or mobility
- Sat — Lower B + finisher
- Sun — Light recovery or optional cardio LISS

Example Week 5 (exact)
Mon — Upper A (Horizontal emphasis)
- Warm‑up 8 min
- Main:
  1) Decline push‑ups (feet elevated) or weighted push‑ups with backpack: 5×4–6 (2–3s eccentric or 2/0/1), rest 90–150 s.
  2) Banded or full pull‑ups: 5×4–6 (or 4×6–8 banded), rest 90–150 s.
  3) Australian rows (harder angle): 4×8–10.
- Accessory: diamond push‑ups 3×8–12; plank 3×45s.
- Finish: mobility 5–8 min.

Tue — Lower A
- Main:
  1) Pistol progressions to a chair: 4×5–8 each leg.
  2) Single‑leg Romanian deadlift (backpack): 4×6–10 each leg.
  3) Elevated split squat: 3×8–10 each.
- Accessory: single leg glute bridge 4×8–12; calf 3×15–25.
- Finish: mobility.

Thu — Upper B (Vertical emphasis)
- Warm‑up: wrist work, pike warm sets
- Main:
  1) Pike push‑ups (feet elevated) or wall handstand negatives: 4–6×4–8 (3s eccentric), rest 90–150 s.
  2) Pull‑ups (weighted or banded): 4×4–6 or 5×3–6 if heavy.
  3) Inverted row superset for balance: 3×8–12.
- Accessory: towel face pulls 3×12–15; hollow holds 3×30s.
- Finish: mobility.

Sat — Lower B + Finisher
- Main:
  1) Jump squat (controlled) 4×6–8.
  2) Elevated single‑leg hip thrust 4×8–10.
  3) Reverse Nordic or hamstring emphasis 3×6–10.
- Accessory: farmer carry backpack 3×60s.
- Finish: Saturday finisher (12–16 min AMRAP/EMOM/Tabata) and cool down.

Progression notes Weeks 6–8
- Week 6: increase heavy sets to 4–5 and incorporate 1–2 paused sets (1–3s) per push exercise.
- Week 7: try harder push variations (archer/one‑arm assisted or heavier decline); add backpack weight if available; increase pull‑up intensity toward unassisted sets of 4–6.
- Week 8: peak Phase 2 intensity — perform 5–6 sets at 3–6 reps for main push/pull progressions. Do an AMRAP test for push (max push‑ups) and pull (max strict pull‑ups) at end of Week 8 to gauge progress.

Phase 3 — Intensify / Peaking (Weeks 9–12)
Goal: raise mechanical tension, lower rep strength work, heavier backpack loading, include deload/test in Week 12.

Key changes
- Rep ranges: 3–6 reps for main strength movements, 4–8 for accessory heavy single‑leg work.
- Sets: increase sets for main lifts (5–6) with longer rests (2–3 min).
- Use backpack or adjustable dumbbells/kettlebell if purchased to add external load.
- Cardio: reduce high intensity if interfering with strength; keep short conditioning sessions.

Weeks 9–11 weekly template
- Mon — Upper A (Strength emphasis heavy pull + heavy horizontal push)
- Tue — Lower A (heavy single‑leg + hinge)
- Wed — optional LISS mobility
- Thu — Upper B (heavy vertical push + pull)
- Fri — rest
- Sat — Lower B + finisher
- Sun — rest or light cardio

Example Week 9 (exact)
Mon — Upper A
- Warm‑up
- Main:
  1) Weighted pull‑ups (backpack) or heavy full pull‑ups: 6×3–6, rest 150–180 s.
  2) Weighted decline/flat push‑ups: 5×5–8 (2s pause), rest 120–150 s.
  3) Australian rows feet elevated: 4×6–8 for heavy pulling.
- Accessory: handstand practice 3×20–40s; L‑sit progressions 3×10–20s.
- Finish: mobility.

Tue — Lower A
- Main:
  1) Weighted pistol progressions or heavy Bulgarian: 5×4–6 per leg.
  2) Heavy backpack RDL: 5×5–8.
  3) Step‑ups heavy: 4×6–8 each.

- Continuous movement at a sustained moderate effort: alternating 5 min brisk in‑place march with 5 min more intense (skipping without rope, quick feet, step‑ups).
- Intensity: slightly breathy but can speak in short sentences (RPE 5–6 / 65–75% max HR).

3) Low‑impact HIIT (knees/step based) — 10–15 min (good for small space)
- Warm‑up 3–4 min.
- 6–8 rounds: 20s hard, 40s easy (work:rest = 1:2). Hard effort examples: fast high knees, squat jumps (if floor/ceiling allows), fast alternating lunge jumps (or static lunges for low impact), mountain climbers.
- Cool‑down 3–4 min.
- Total time ~12–18 min. RPE 7–9 during work intervals.

4) Classic Tabata (if fit and no joint issues) — 4 min intense + warm‑up/cool‑down
- 20s all‑out, 10s rest × 8. Exercises: burpees, squat jumps, fast mountain climbers, or squat pulses. Use only 1–2 rounds per week because of intensity.

5) EMOM bodyweight circuit (conditioning + core)
- 20 min EMOM (every minute on the minute): Minute 1: 12–16 air squats; Minute 2: 8–12 push‑ups; Minute 3: 12–16 mountain climbers (per side counted as 1); Minute 4: 30s plank. Rest remaining time each minute. Keeps heart rate elevated and trains work capacity.

6) Stair or step workout (if building has stairs)
- 10–30 min of continuous stair walking or step‑ups (2:1 work:rest or steady pace). Great for conditioning and low impact.

Sample weekly cardio templates (match to goals)

B) Balanced (strength + fat‑loss)

- Sun: 12–15 min HIIT (low‑impact).
- Optionally add 10–15 min LISS after one strength session.

C) Fat‑loss priority (more cardio)

- Fri: 20–25 min MISS (step‑based).
- Sun: 12–15 min HIIT.

Progression examples across 12 weeks
- Weeks 1–4 (foundation): 2×/week LISS 20–30 min; 1×/week 10‑12 min low‑impact HIIT starting week 3 if recovered.
- Weeks 5–8 (build): increase one LISS to 30–40 min or add an extra MISS session; HIIT intensity or rounds ++ (e.g., 8 rounds).
- Weeks 9–11 (intensify): keep 1–2 HIIT sessions/week (short) and 1 LISS 30–40 min; watch recovery and reduce if strength suffers.
- Week 12 (deload/test): cut cardio volume by 40–60% and avoid HIIT during the testing week; preserve freshness for strength tests.

How to monitor and adjust
- Track RPE and recovery: if strength drops or client feels excessively sore/fatigued, reduce cardio frequency or intensity.
- If goal is fat loss and weight isn’t moving after 2 weeks, increase LISS duration by 10 min or add another short HIIT session; better first to adjust diet before dramatically increasing cardio.
- Use perceived exertion and breathing: LISS = conversational pace. HIIT = hard, non‑sustainable intervals.

- 5 min cool‑down and stretch.

Good question — for a client training in a small flat who currently has only a doorway pull‑up bar and mat, smart, compact additions will greatly expand progression options and speed strength gains. Below is a prioritized, practical equipment list with recommended types, suggested weight ranges, and why each item helps. I focus on space‑efficient, budget‑sensible choices that let you add load to pull‑ups, squats, hinges, carries, and presses.

Priority 1 — A solid adjustable backpack or heavy duffel (first, cheapest upgrade)
- Why: Extremely versatile — can be loaded with books, sandbags, water bottles, or grocery bags to add weight for pull‑ups, push‑ups, squats, lunges, RDLs, carries and rows.
- What to buy: A sturdy hiking backpack or military‑style rucksack with chest/waist straps; aim for 30–50 L capacity.
- Recommended max load: should feel comfortable up to 20–30+ kg when distributed.
- Cost/space: Low, small footprint; you likely already have one.

Priority 2 — Adjustable dumbbells (best single purchase for space and versatility)
- Why: Allow safe progressive loading for almost every upper and lower body lift (rows, split squats, Romanian DLs, weighted carries, presses, curls). Space‑efficient and easy to store.
- What to buy: Adjustable dumbbells (selector or plate‑style). Choose a pair that adjusts up to at least 20–40 kg total per dumbbell depending on client strength and budget.
  - If budget/space limited: get adjustable pair up to ~20–25 kg each (44–55 lb each) — sufficient for most beginners to intermediates for many movements.
  - If you can spend more: get up to 40 kg (88 lb) per dumbbell to avoid needing new equipment later.
- Cost/space: Moderate cost; low storage footprint.

Priority 3 — A single adjustable kettlebell or set of 2 (very useful for swings, carries, goblet squats)
- Why: Kettlebells are ideal for hip hinge power (swings), loaded carries, goblet squats, single‑arm rows and presses.
- What to buy: One adjustable kettlebell or a few fixed weights. For beginners, a 8–16 kg kettlebell is useful; add 20–24 kg later.
- Cost/space: Small footprint; moderate cost.

Priority 4 — A compact pair of weight plates + a simple bar (optional)
- Why: If you want heavier loading for squats/deadlifts and the client progresses beyond dumbbells, plates + short bar let you create heavier loads without bulky barbells.
- What to buy: 2–4 plates of 5–10 kg and a short strong loadable bar (or thick dumbbell handles to make heavier farmer's holds).
- Cost/space: Low‑moderate.

Priority 5 — Resistance bands (loop and long/thick bands)
- Why: Extremely versatile, cheap, take almost no space. Use for assisted pull‑ups, banded pull‑throughs, rows, press assistance, mobility and stretching.
- What to buy: A set including light, medium, heavy loop bands plus a long heavy band for pull‑up assistance. Get a band anchoring strap or door anchor if needed.
- Cost/space: Low.

Priority 6 — Foldable plyo box or sturdy step / small bench (multi‑use)
- Why: Step‑ups, elevated split squats, box jumps (if ceiling allows), elevated push‑ups, Bulgarian split squat support. Useful for progressions.
- What to buy: A low‑profile, collapsible plyo box/bench or a sturdy step stool. Height range 20–24 in (50–60 cm) ideally with 2 heights or adjustable.
- Cost/space: Moderate; choose foldable or stackable options.

Optional higher‑level gear (if budget & space allow)
- Sandbag (adjustable fill): great for awkward loading and carries.
- Compact barbell set with bumper or iron plates and a short barbell (if you have floor space and neighbor considerations).
- Pull‑up bar with dip handles or free‑standing rig (not necessary if doorway bar works).

Recommended first purchases and suggested order (for a beginner in a small flat)
1) Backpack/duffel + heavy books or water bottles (immediate, <$50) — allows quick weighted progressions.
2) Resistance band set (assist + heavy band) — <$30.
3) Adjustable dumbbells up to ~20–25 kg each (or a pair of fixed dumbbells if cheaper) — $100–300 depending on brand.
4) Kettlebell 12–16 kg (or adjustable kettlebell) — $40–120.
5) Small foldable step/box — $30–100.
Later: upgrade adjustable dumbbells to heavier set (up to 40 kg each) or add plates/bar if client outgrows them.

What weights to buy specifically (practical buyer recommendations)
- If buying only one compact set: adjustable dumbbells that go 2.5–25 kg (5–55 lb) per dumbbell. Brands vary by country; pick one with secure locking and lifetime warranty if possible.
- If buying kettlebells: start with 12 kg and 16 kg fixed (or adjustable set covering 8–24 kg).
- If buying plates: 2 x 5 kg + 2 x 10 kg plates and a short 1.2 m bar — handy for farmer carries and heavier loads.

How much load will he need eventually?
- For most beginners progressing to intermediate strength, being able to load 20–40 kg in one implement (dumbbell, kettlebell, backpack) for single‑leg/single‑arm work and 30–60+ kg for two‑handed deadlift/squat patterns is typical.
- Example milestones where equipment matters:
  - Pull‑ups: once bodyweight pull‑ups are solid, adding 5–15 kg in a backpack helps build strength.
  - Squats/hinges: single‑leg Bulgarian squats and RDLs will rapidly require 10–30+ kg to continue progressing.
  - Carries: progressive farmer carries with 20–40+ kg total (split across hands) are excellent for full‑body strength.

Space, noise, and neighbor considerations
- Use rubber mats or a piece of carpet under weights to reduce noise and protect floors.
- Avoid heavy barbell drops in flats; prefer controlled lifts, dumbbells and kettlebells.
- Consider training times considerate of neighbors when doing noisy carries or jumps.

Budget examples

- Mid budget (~$200–$500): Adjustable dumbbells (to ~20–25 kg each) + bands + step.

Final recommendation (single best buy for biggest return)
- If you can buy only one thing: adjustable dumbbells (pair) with a working range up to ~20–25 kg each. They provide the broadest exercise carryover and allow steady progression from beginner to intermediate in a small flat.

Do you mean: increase the difficulty/intensity of the push (push‑up / vertical push) work during Phase 2 (Weeks 5–8)? Or do you mean adjust overall training intensity for all pushing patterns across Phase 2? 

I’ll assume you mean increasing the push (horizontal and vertical pushing) intensity during Phase 2. Below I give a clear plan you can apply throughout Weeks 5–8: specific progressions, set/rep targets, tempo and rest, weekly ramping, examples to use with only a pull‑up bar, mat and added backpack/bands, and ways to monitor / scale if he’s fatiguing.

Key goals for push intensity in Phase 2
- Shift from high‑volume foundational work to higher mechanical tension: fewer reps per set, harder variations, added pauses/slow eccentrics, and some increased overall weekly push volume to stimulate strength gains without compromising recovery.
- Improve both horizontal push (push‑ups) and vertical push (pike push / handstand progressions) strength and transfer to one‑arm push progression later.

What to change compared with Phase 1
- Move from 4×8–15 higher‑rep sets to 4–6 sets of 4–8 reps on the hardest variation for the session, or 4×6–12 when using slower tempo for added time under tension.
- Increase intensity via: elevation (decline), unilateral variations (incline archer → archer → one‑arm negatives), added pause at the bottom (1–3 s), and slower eccentrics (3–5 s). Use backpack to add external load for experienced clients.
- Increase rest between sets for the heaviest push sets to 90–150 s to allow greater strength output.
- Retain 1–2 accessory higher‑rep sets per session for volume and hypertrophy (e.g., diamond push‑ups, close grip push‑ups) but keep them submaximal (stop 1–2 reps short of failure).

Specific weekly structure for push intensity (Weeks 5–8)
- Frequency: 2 push sessions per week (Upper A + Upper B). One session focuses on heavier horizontal push; the other emphasizes vertical push and challenging variations.
- Rep ranges and sets:
  - Heavy sets: 4–6 sets × 4–6 reps (or 5×3–6 for very hard variations) with 2–3 min rest.
  - Moderate sets for time under tension: 3–4 sets × 6–10 reps with 3–4 s eccentrics or 1–2 s pause.
  - Accessory hypertrophy sets: 2–3 sets × 8–15 reps with 45–75 s rest.
- Tempo examples:
  - Heavy strength: 2/0/1 (2s eccentric, no pause, explosive concentric) or 3/0/1 for added tension.
  - Paused variant: 3/1/1 (3s down, 1s pause, explode up).
  - Slow TUT variant: 4/0/2 or 5/0/1 for eccentric emphasis.
- RPE: Aim for RPE 7–9 on heavy sets (stop 0–2 reps shy of technical failure). Accessory sets RPE 6–7.

Progressions to use (choose appropriate based on current ability)
- Horizontal push progressions (easier → harder):
  1) Incline push‑up (hands elevated)
  2) Standard push‑up
  3) Decline push‑up (feet elevated)
  4) Close/diamond push‑up (for triceps emphasis)
  5) Archer push‑up (unilateral emphasis)
  6) One‑arm assisted push‑up (offset weight or band assist)
  7) One‑arm negative / one‑arm push‑up
  8) Weighted push‑up (backpack)
- Vertical push progressions (easier → harder):
  1) Wall‑facing pike push‑up progression (incline pike)
  2) Pike push‑up (feet on floor, hips high)
  3) Decline pike (feet elevated)
  4) Wall handstand hold (partial weight on hands)
  5) Wall handstand push‑up negatives
  6) Partial ROM handstand push‑ups (with cushion)
  7) Full handstand push‑ups or weighted variations

How to structure the two weekly push sessions in Phase 2

Session 1 — Horizontal push emphasis (heavier)
- Warm‑up: shoulder mobility, scapular push‑ups 2×8, light push‑up set 1×10.
- Main:
  1) Hardest horizontal push variation (e.g., decline push‑up or archer): 5 sets × 4–6 reps, tempo 2/0/1 or 3/0/1, rest 90–150 s.
  2) Secondary push movement (close grip or weighted push‑up): 3 sets × 6–8 reps, tempo 3/1/1 (pause), rest 90 s.
- Accessory:
  3) Inverted row or doorway row superset with push (maintain horizontal push/pull balance) 3×8–12.
  4) Triceps focused: bench dips (use chair) 3×8–15 or diamond push‑ups 3×8–12.
- Core: 2–3 sets plank variations 30–60 s.
- Optional finisher: 1 set to near‑failure of a lighter push (e.g., knee push‑ups) to accumulate volume — keep it short.

Session 2 — Vertical push emphasis (skill + strength)
- Warm‑up: wrist mobility, pike push‑up warm sets 2×6, wall walks if safe.
- Main:
  1) Pike push‑up progression or wall handstand negative: 4–6 sets × 4–8 reps, tempo 3/0/1 (or 3/1/1 for paused at head), rest 90–150 s.
  2) Bench/step elevated pike or assisted one‑arm negatives (if working on unilateral strength): 3 sets × 5–8 each side as appropriate, tempo 3/0/1, rest 90 s.
- Accessory:
  3) Overhead pressing carryover — pike push to partial handstand press negatives: 3×4–6 (skill).
  4) Scapular work / face pulls with towel 3×12–15.
- Core/shoulder health: 3×10–15 bandless or towel face pulls, scapular retractions.

Weekly ramp (how to increase intensity each week weeks 5–8)
- Week 5: Establish stronger variations at moderate reps (4–8). Use 3–4 sets for main heavy lift.
- Week 6: Increase sets to 4–5 for main heavy lift and add pauses/longer eccentrics on 1 set per exercise.
- Week 7: Increase intensity — attempt harder variation (decline → archer; pike → wall negatives) while keeping reps in 4–6 range. Keep rest longer (2–3 min).
- Week 8: Peak intensity week for Phase 2 — perform 5–6 sets of the hardest workable variation at 3–6 reps, with one heavier set (or single AMRAP set where appropriate) to test progression. Keep accessory volume moderate to preserve recovery.

Using backpack or bands to increase load
- Backpack: add 2.5–10+ kg for push sets as appropriate. Add small weight increments; use only if client can maintain bracing and form.
- Bands: loop band across upper back for extra resistance on push‑ups (safer alternative to backpack for precise progressive tension).

Monitoring fatigue and scaling back
- If push performance drops across sessions (not progressing, fewer reps or RPE increases by >1–2), reduce heavy set volume by 1 set or use slightly easier variation.
- Maintain at least 48 hours between the hardest vertical push session and heavy shoulder/upper body work.
- If shoulder pain occurs, regress to easier variations, increase rotator cuff and scapular stability work (face pulls, Y/T raises, external rotation with towel), and reduce eccentric load temporarily.

Examples for a client with limited equipment
- Horizontal heavy day: Decline push‑ups 5×5 (2/0/1) + close push‑ups 3×8 (3/1/1) + rows 3×8–12.
- Vertical heavy day: Wall handstand negatives 4–6×4 (3/0/1) or Pike push‑ups feet elevated 5×5 + towel face pulls 3×15.

Progress checks and criteria to advance
- Move up to a harder horizontal push variation when the client completes 5×6 of current variation in two consecutive sessions with good form.
- For vertical push, progress from pike to wall negatives when client can do 4×6 strict pike reps with controlled tempo and bracing.
- Use one AMRAP (as many reps as possible) set on week 8 of Phase 2 to check progress (e.g., max strict push‑ups or max pike push‑up reps); record and compare to Phase 1.

Sample week (Week 6) with exact push prescription
- Mon (Upper A horizontal emphasis):
  - Decline push‑ups: 5 sets × 5 reps (3s down, no pause, explode up), rest 120 s.
  - Close push‑ups: 3×8 (2s pause at bottom), rest 90 s.
  - Inverted row: 3×10, rest 60–90 s.
  - Plank: 3×45 s.
- Thu (Upper B vertical emphasis):
  - Pike push‑ups (feet elevated on low step): 5×5 (3/0/1), rest 120 s.
  - Assisted one‑arm push‑up negatives: 3×5 each side (slow), rest 90–120 s.
  - Towel face pulls: 3×15.
  - Hollow holds: 3×30 s.

Summary checklist for the trainer to implement Phase 2 push intensity
- Move to 4–6 sets of 4–6 reps on the hardest variation twice weekly.
- Use slow eccentrics (3–5 s) and 1–3 s pauses to increase time under tension.
- Rest 90–150 s between heavy sets.
- Progress via elevation, unilateral work, pauses, tempo and backpack/band loading.
- Keep accessory sets moderate volume and submaximal to avoid overreaching.
- Monitor recovery and back off if technique degrades or RPE rises significantly.

Below is a simple, practical mobility routine your client can use daily (10–20 minutes) to support the 12‑week strength program. It’s built for a small flat, needs only a mat and a wall (or doorway), and targets the main areas stressed by the program: shoulders/thoracic spine, hips, hamstrings, ankles, and thoracic/neck. I give a short daily routine (10 minutes) and a longer session (15–20 minutes) he can do on recovery days or after workouts. Each drill includes purpose, how to perform, reps/time, and coaching cues.

Daily quick routine — 10 minutes (ideal post‑warm‑up or evening)
Purpose: maintain joint mobility, reduce stiffness, improve posture and recovery.

1) Diaphragmatic breathing + pelvic tilts — 90 s
- How: Lying on back or seated. 4–6 deep diaphragmatic breaths, expand belly on inhale, draw navel toward spine on exhale. Follow each 3 breaths with 5 slow pelvic tilts (rock pelvis posterior/anterior).
- Coaching: focus on deep belly breathing, slow movement to activate core and relax hips.

2) Shoulder/pec opener on doorway — 60 s each side
- How: Place forearm on door frame at shoulder height or slightly higher, step forward to feel a gentle stretch in chest/shoulder.
- Coaching: keep torso upright, avoid twisting. Softly lean until you feel a stretch, hold 60 s each side.

3) Thoracic spine rotation (kneeling or standing) — 8–10 reps each side
- How: On knees or standing, hands behind head, rotate thoracic to one side while keeping hips stable. Or lying on side open/close top arm.
- Coaching: move through the upper back, not the lower back. Aim for controlled range.

4) Bandless face‑pull / scapular retraction (towel or imaginary band) — 2 sets × 10–12
- How: Hold a towel with both hands, elbows high, simulate pulling to face height squeezing scapulae together. Slow and controlled.
- Coaching: reinforce shoulder blade control and posture.

5) World's Greatest Stretch (Lunge + twist) — 6–8 reps each side
- How: Step into a deep lunge, drop back knee to mat if needed, place opposite elbow inside front foot then rotate torso toward the front leg reaching up. Return and switch.
- Coaching: move slowly, aim for thoracic rotation and hip flexor stretch.

6) Couch stretch / kneeling hip flexor stretch — 60 s each side
- How: Kneel with back knee on mat and torso upright, drive hips forward to stretch front of hip. If possible, tuck back foot under a couch or use wall for deeper stretch.
- Coaching: posterior tilt to protect low back, squeeze glute of front leg.

7) Hamstring bandless stretch (single‑leg lying or seated reach) — 45–60 s each side
- How: On back, one leg straight up, keep knee soft, actively pull toes toward you to deepen. Or sit and reach.
- Coaching: aim for gentle tension, not pain.

8) Ankle dorsiflexion mobilization (knee-to-wall) — 8–10 reps each side
- How: Face a wall, place foot 5–10 cm from wall, bend knee toward wall keeping heel down; adjust distance to reach 8–10 reps.
- Coaching: keep heel on floor and move slowly; helps squat depth and landing mechanics.

Short version structure (10 min): Breathing/pelvic tilts (90s) → doorway pec stretch (1 min per side) → thoracic rotations (1.5 min) → World's Greatest Stretch (2 min) → hamstring (1.5 min) → ankle mobilization (1 min).

Longer recovery session — 15–20 minutes (use on rest days or after workouts)
Purpose: deeper mobility and soft tissue work, longer holds, and strengthening through range.

1) 2‑3 minutes: Diaphragmatic breathing + pelvic tilts + knee hugs (limp back mobility)
- Same as quick routine but longer breathing focus.

2) 90–120 s per side: Couch stretch with glute activation
- How: perform the kneeling hip flexor stretch but add a 3–5s glute squeeze at end range, 6–8 slow breaths.
- Coaching: activate glute to protect pelvis, breathe into the stretch.

3) 60–90 s per side: Pigeon or half‑pigeon variation (modified if hips tight)
- How: From tabletop, bring one knee forward and drop shin diagonally; keep torso upright or fold forward for deeper stretch.
- Coaching: move within pain‑free range; 6–8 deep breaths.

4) 2 sets × 6–8 reps each side: 90/90 hip internal/external rotation flow
- How: Seated or lying, start with hips at 90/90 and switch to opposite rotation in controlled manner.
- Coaching: focus on hip joint motion rather than low back.

5) 2 sets × 6–10 reps: Thoracic extension over chair or rolled towel
- How: Place rolled towel or yoga mat rolled under thoracic spine and gently extend over it, hands behind head, small controlled reps.
- Coaching: limit to pain‑free range; keep neck neutral.

6) 2 sets × 10–12 reps: Cat/cow + thread the needle (spinal mobility)
- How: On hands & knees, alternate arching/rounding, then thread one arm under body and rotate to open chest.
- Coaching: move slowly and breathe.

7) 2 sets × 8–12 reps: Shoulder 90/90 external rotation with towel (strengthening through range)
- How: Lie on side, elbows at 90, rotate forearm upward keeping elbow against torso — use light resistance from other hand or towel.
- Coaching: reinforce rotator cuff control.

8) 2 sets × 8–12 reps: Glute med activation (clamshells) + single‑leg bridge 8–10 each
- How: Lying on side, knees bent, open top knee (clamshell). Follow with single‑leg glute bridge on back.
- Coaching: control movement, avoid lumbar overextension.

9) 60–90 s each side: Active hamstring and calf flossing (knee straightening + ankle mobilization)
- How: Standing or seated, actively dorsiflex ankle and lift toes toward shin while straightening knee; repeat to mobilize posterior chain.

10) Finish 2–3 min: Shoulder mobility flow with wall slides + deep breathing
- How: Stand against a wall, perform slow wall slides maintaining contact and scapular control; pair with controlled breathing.
- Coaching: keep low back neutral; if wall contact impossible, do floor slides.

Daily reminders and coaching cues
- Aim for daily 10‑minute routine and longer 15–20 minute mobility 2–3×/week.
- Breathe: long slow breaths increase relaxation and allow deeper, safer mobility.
- Move within pain‑free ranges. Sharp joint pain = stop and regress.
- Load the mobility with activation: combine stretches with glute activation or scapular retractions to build strength through the range.
- Consistency > intensity: small daily mobility beats sporadic long sessions.

How to integrate with the 12‑week plan
- Before lifting: 5–7 minutes of dynamic mobility (ankle mobilization, world’s greatest stretch, scapular activation, 1–2 light movement sets).
- After lifting: 5–10 minutes of the quick routine focusing on the areas worked that day (e.g., shoulders & thoracic after upper day; hips & hamstrings after lower day).
- Recovery days: use the longer 15–20 minute session or active recovery walks + mobility.

Below is a single, coach‑friendly 12‑week program you can give your 27‑year‑old beginner client training in a small flat with only a yoga mat and a doorway pull‑up bar. It integrates the strength plan (progressive bodyweight + backpack loading), nutrition guidance, at‑home cardio, push intensity in Phase 2, Saturday finisher, equipment buying path, and daily mobility. I present a week‑by‑week summary with session breakdowns, progression rules, and practical coaching notes so you can deliver it remotely.

Quick overview
- Frequency: 4 strength sessions/week + Saturday finisher. Optional cardio on Wed and/or Sun depending on goals.
- Split: Upper A (Mon), Lower A (Tue), Upper B (Thu), Lower B (Sat morning) + Saturday finisher (later) OR Lower B + finisher same day (shorter). Mobility daily (short) + longer 1–2× week.
- Phases:
  - Phase 1 Foundation: Weeks 1–4 — build movement patterns, volume, technique.
  - Phase 2 Build: Weeks 5–8 — increase push intensity, harder variations, more mechanical tension.
  - Phase 3 Intensify/Peak: Weeks 9–12 — lower‑rep strength emphasis, backpack loading, deload/test Week 12.
- Equipment: mat + pull‑up bar. Recommended purchases across program: backpack, resistance bands, adjustable dumbbells/kettlebells later (see Equipment section).
- Nutrition: three options (surplus for strength, maintenance, deficit). Protein 1.6–2.2 g/kg, creatine 3–5 g/day optional. If you provide his bodyweight I will customise exact kcal/macros.

Progression rules (use weekly)
- Progress when client completes upper target reps/sets with good form for 2 consecutive sessions.
- If stuck, increase volume (more sets), extend eccentric tempo, or add backpack/band assistance/resistance.
- Monitor RPE and recovery; back off volume if performance drops or sleep/energy suffers.

How to read daily session entries
- Warm‑up: 5–8 min dynamic warm‑up each session.
- Main: core strength movements with sets × reps and tempo or cues.
- Accessory: supporting movements for balance/hypertrophy.

- Increase reps/sets slightly and aim for improving technique. Start moving assisted pull‑up -> banded or partial concentric + eccentric. Add one extra set to main lifts on Week 4 if recovery permits.

Goal: increase intensity, especially push work (set/rep reductions, harder variations, pauses/slow eccentrics), increase single‑leg and pulling intensity.

Key changes from Phase 1
- Push intensity: two push sessions/week with 4–6 sets of 4–6 reps on hardest variation; slow eccentrics, 1–3s pauses, rest 90–150 s (detailed push progressions implemented).
- Pulls: progress to more full pull‑ups, banded or unassisted, increase sets.
- Lower: progress toward single‑leg pistols, heavier single‑leg RDLs with backpack.
- Cardio: increase to 2 sessions/week (one LISS + one short HIIT) if conditioning/fat loss is goal; otherwise keep 1 LISS.

- Sets: increase sets for main lifts (5–6) with longer rests (2–3 min).

- Testing: after a light warm‑up, test:

  - Max push‑up reps in one set (strict form).
  - Single‑leg pistol or loaded single‑leg rep test as safe.
- Avoid all‑out HIIT; keep mobility and recovery focus.

- Emphasise scapular control on pulls and pushes, neutral spine on hinges, knees tracking toes on lunges, controlled eccentrics.

- Keep sleep, hydration and nutrition monitored.
